title: Allylic bromination with NBS
subtitle: Cyclohexene and N-bromosuccinimide give 3-bromocyclohexene through an allylic radical

reactants.caption: cyclohexene + bromine radical (NBS in the flask)
reactants.learnerPrompt: Use fish-hook arrows: each moves one electron. The bromine radical takes a hydrogen from cyclohexene.
hintTiers: Which C–H bond of cyclohexene is weakest? Breaking it should give the most stable radical.
The bromine radical takes an allylic hydrogen, one on the carbon next to the C=C. The C–H bond splits evenly. Three fish-hooks.
Bromine's unpaired electron → new Br–H bond; one electron of the allylic C–H bond → Br–H; the other → the allylic carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Br• can add to the C=C, but that addition is reversible, and with so little Br₂ present the radical formed falls apart again. Abstraction of the weak allylic C–H wins.
Br• can add to the C=C, but that addition is reversible, and with so little Br₂ present the radical formed falls apart again. Abstraction of the weak allylic C–H wins.
That carbon already has four bonds. A radical abstracts a hydrogen, which can only make one bond.
NBS is not attacked by the radical here. Its job is polar: it turns the HBr formed into Br₂. Start with the alkene's weakest C–H bond.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: One electron is missing: the new H–Br bond needs two, one from Br• and one from the C–H bond.

allyl-radical.caption: allylic radical + Br₂ (from NBS) + succinimide
allyl-radical.learnerPrompt: The unpaired electron is not stuck on one carbon. Draw the other resonance form of the allylic radical.
hintTiers: A radical next to a C=C is delocalised. Which electrons can move without breaking any σ bond?
The unpaired electron pairs with one electron of the C=C π bond to make a new π bond; the other π electron ends on the far carbon. Three fish-hooks.
Unpaired electron → new π bond to its neighbour; one electron of the old π bond → the same new π bond; the other → the far end carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Bonding the two ends of the allyl unit would make a three-membered ring. Resonance moves electrons only: the σ bonds stay put.
That is how Br₂ adds to an alkene by the polar route. NBS keeps Br₂ so dilute that this addition is too slow; the radical chain wins.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: One more fish-hook: the new π bond needs two electrons, one from the radical and one from the old π bond.

allyl-radical-other-form.caption: the other resonance form: unpaired electron on the other end
allyl-radical-other-form.learnerPrompt: The radical takes a bromine atom from Br₂.
hintTiers: The Br–Br bond is weak. Which atom does the carbon radical attack?
The carbon radical makes a bond to one bromine while the Br–Br bond splits evenly. Three fish-hooks.
Carbon's unpaired electron → new C–Br bond; one Br–Br electron → C–Br; the other → the far bromine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: There is no HBr left on screen: NBS has turned it into Br₂. The radical reacts with Br₂.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: One more fish-hook: the new C–Br bond needs an electron from the Br–Br bond as well.

steps.explanationAfterStep: The allylic C–H bond (about 360 kJ mol⁻¹) is much weaker than the other C–H bonds (about 410–465), because the radical formed is delocalised over three carbons.

steps.caption: NBS reacts with the HBr just formed (a polar reaction) to give Br₂ and succinimide.

steps.explanationAfterStep: The unpaired electron is spread over both ends of the allyl unit: two resonance forms of one radical. This delocalisation is why the allylic C–H was the one broken.
Either end of the allylic radical can take the bromine; in cyclohexene both ends are equivalent, so there is one product. The new Br• abstracts the next allylic hydrogen: a chain.
Also correct: the radical can take bromine at the carbon where it was drawn. The two ends are equivalent here, so the product is the same 3-bromocyclohexene.

mechanismSummary: A bromine radical abstracts an allylic hydrogen, giving a delocalised allylic radical. NBS reacts with the HBr formed to give Br₂, but only ever a little at a time. The allylic radical takes a bromine atom from Br₂, giving 3-bromocyclohexene and a new bromine radical, so the chain continues. Because Br₂ stays dilute, the polar addition of Br₂ across the C=C cannot compete.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 37 (Radical reactions)
